analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 tax cuts permanent and cuts the top capital gains tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill to make the 2001 tax cuts permanent and cut the top capital gains rate to 15% never left the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law (EGTRRA) lowered income tax rates for most taxpayers, but Congress included a "sunset" so the cuts would expire after 2010. This bill would erase that expiration date, making the cuts permanent, and would cut the top capital gains tax rate from 20% to 15% (and to 7.5% for lower-bracket gains), including under the alternative minimum tax. The bill was introduced by Sen. Phil Gramm in October 2001, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: All households that pay federal income tax would keep the 2001 rate reductions permanently, since the 2010 expiration date would be erased. The largest dollar benefits, though, would go to high-income households: they hold most of the appreciated assets subject to capital gains tax, so cutting the top rate from 20% to 15% and to 7.5% at the bottom would send the biggest checks to people with large investment income. Investors and the financial services industry would also gain from a lower tax on asset sales.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2010 sunset date in the 2001 tax law (EGTRRA), so the individual income tax rate reductions and other tax changes would not expire — keeping in place, permanently, the lower rates enacted for all income-tax payers.
Cuts the top capital gains tax rate for individuals from 20% to 15%, and to 7.5% for gains that fall in the lower tax brackets, for tax years ending after December 31, 2001.
Applies the same 15% capital gains rate inside the alternative minimum tax calculation, so taxpayers exposed to the AMT would also get the reduced rate on their gains.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury pays first: the bill has no revenue offsets, so making the cuts permanent and cutting capital gains rates reduces government revenue indefinitely, adding to deficits or forcing future spending cuts or tax increases. Because capital gains income is concentrated among the wealthy, the lost revenue would be recovered later from a broader base — ordinary taxpayers through borrowing costs, reduced services, or future taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Future taxpayers and the federal treasury

drawbacks.text: The bill has no revenue offsets: making the 2001 tax cuts permanent and cutting capital gains rates would reduce federal revenue indefinitely, adding to deficits or requiring later spending cuts or tax increases to fill the gap.

The capital gains cut delivers its largest dollar benefits to households with substantial investment income, which is concentrated among high earners; ordinary households holding little in appreciated assets gain little from it.

By repealing the 2010 sunset entirely, the bill removes the mechanism Congress had used to keep the 2001 tax law within budget rules, locking in the revenue loss permanently rather than debating it later with fuller information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real tax cuts to most households by making the 2001 rate reductions permanent, and its backers argued permanence and lower capital gains taxes would encourage investment during the 2001 recession. The serious cost is its design: nothing in the bill pays for either change, so the entire amount becomes added federal debt or requires future spending cuts or tax increases — and the distribution tilts sharply toward the wealthiest households, since top earners hold most income taxed at the top rates and own most appreciated capital assets. As drafted, the largest benefits flow to those with the most investment income, while the financing burden is deferred to everyone.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Phil Gramm introduced the Economic Revitalization Tax Cut Act in the Senate on October 3, 2001.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the committee that handles tax legislation.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a vote on the Senate floor, and it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
Only 4 senators signed on as cosponsors — 3 Republicans and 1 Democrat — signaling very limited support in the chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the largest capital gains tax cut it promised never went to high-income investors, and the federal government avoided an unoffset, permanent revenue loss. The George W. Bush administration's broader effort to extend the 2001 tax cuts succeeded separately in later years, but this bill itself went nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal treasury; high-income investors did not gain

for.name: Phil Gramm
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 3, 2001 to repeal the 2010 sunset on the 2001 tax cuts and cut capital gains rates.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 3, 2001 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with 3 Republican and 1 Democratic cosponsor, and since it never reached the floor there was no vote to show how the parties would have divided.

industries.note: Capital gains income is heavily concentrated among the wealthiest households, so cutting the top rate from 20% to 15% — and making it apply under the alternative minimum tax — delivers the largest dollar benefit to them. If the bill passed, the widest share of the tax savings would go to households already at the top of the income distribution.

Lower capital gains rates increase the after-tax return on buying and selling assets, which encourages more trading and asset management activity and supports fees for brokers, fund managers, and financial advisers. The benefit to ordinary savers is secondhand and much smaller than the benefit to large investors.

Making the 2001 rate reductions permanent keeps a modest tax cut in place for most people who pay income tax, which helps ordinary households somewhat. But because the bill contains no offsets, the lost revenue becomes debt or future pressure for spending cuts, and the largest share of the total savings accrues to top earners.
